explanation:
Step 1: Read the attendance values
— VI 88/86/92, VII 82/90/88, VIII 90/85/94, IX 84/80/90, X 92/88/91 (July/August/September)
Step 2: Apply the August condition
— At least 85% in August: VI (86), VII (90), VIII (85), X (88); IX (80) drops out
Step 3: Apply the September condition
— At least 90% in September: VI (92), VIII (94), X (91); VII (88) drops out
Step 4: Average the July values
— July: VI 88, VIII 90, X 92
— Average = (88 + 90 + 92) ÷ 3 = 270 ÷ 3 = 90%
Step 5: Check a slip
— Keeping VII by mistake gives (88 + 82 + 90 + 92) ÷ 4 = 88%, a wrong option
∴ Correct answer: (B) 90%
trick: Apply both conditions one by one, then average only the classes that pass both.

explanation:
Step 1: Write the data
— Rated power P = 60 W, rated voltage V = 240 V
Step 2: Choose the formula
— P = V² ÷ R, so R = V² ÷ P
Step 3: Substitute
— R = 240 × 240 ÷ 60 = 57,600 ÷ 60
Step 4: Result
— R = 960 Ω
Step 5: Check
— Current = P ÷ V = 60 ÷ 240 = 0.25 A; V ÷ I = 240 ÷ 0.25 = 960 Ω, the same
∴ Correct answer: (A) 960 Ω
trick: For a rated lamp use R = V² ÷ P directly.

explanation:
Step 1: Read the bars
— A 115/128/142, B 165/152/171, C 88/104/112, D 146/133/121, E 98/111/107 (2022/2023/2024)
Step 2: Check 2023 against 2022
— Declines in 2023: B (165 to 152) and D (146 to 133)
Step 3: Check 2024 against 2023
— Declines in 2024: D (133 to 121) and E (111 to 107); B climbs to 171
Step 4: Depot declining in both years
— Only D declines in 2023 and in 2024
Step 5: Answer
— D only
∴ Correct answer: (A) D only
trick: A decline in each year means every bar of the depot is shorter than the one before it.

explanation:
Step 1: Read the values
— P 32/36/42/47, S 21/27/33/31, R 41/39/46/52 (2021 to 2024, hundreds)
Step 2: Condition on P
— P at least 36: 2022, 2023, 2024
Step 3: Condition on S
— S at least 31: 2023 (33) and 2024 (31); 2022 fails with 27
Step 4: Add R for 2023 and 2024
— 46 + 52 = 98 hundred = 9,800 fans
Step 5: Check a slip
— Taking 2022 too gives 39 + 46 + 52 = 137 hundred, the trap option
∴ Correct answer: (D) 9,800
trick: Shortlist the years by both conditions first; then add only R.

explanation:
Step 1: Read the values
— Monday 165, Tuesday 210, Wednesday 240, Thursday 185, Friday 290, Saturday 130
Step 2: Find the total
— 165 + 210 + 240 + 185 + 290 + 130 = 1,220
Step 3: Find the share of Friday
— 290 ÷ 1,220 × 100 = 23.77%
Step 4: Round off
— 23.77% ≈ 24%
Step 5: Check
— One-fourth of 1,220 is 305, a little more than 290, so the share is a little under 25%
∴ Correct answer: (C) 24%
trick: Share = part ÷ total × 100; compare with a quarter of the total to check.

explanation:
Step 1: Read the March column
— P 340, Q 410, R 285, S 375, T 360
Step 2: Arrange in decreasing order
— Q 410, S 375, T 360, P 340, R 285
Step 3: Pick the third place
— Third = T (360)
Step 4: Check the neighbours
— S (375) is second and P (340) is fourth, so T is third
Step 5: Answer
— T
∴ Correct answer: (A) T
trick: Use only the column asked for; the other months are distractors.

explanation:
Step 1: State the rule
— A body floats in a liquid if its density is less than that of the liquid, and sinks if it is more
Step 2: Compare the sleeper
— Wood 800 kg/m³ is less than water 1,000 kg/m³, so the sleeper floats
Step 3: Compare the bolt
— Iron 7,800 kg/m³ is more than 1,000 kg/m³, so the bolt sinks
Step 4: Combine
— The sleeper floats and the bolt sinks
Step 5: Link to daily life
— This is why wooden logs float down a river while iron nails sink
∴ Correct answer: (A) The sleeper floats and the bolt sinks
trick: Less dense than the liquid: floats; denser: sinks.

explanation:
Step 1: Price after the first reduction
— 12,500 × 0.84 = ₹10,500
Step 2: Find the cost price
— 10,500 = 1.25 × CP, so CP = 10,500 ÷ 1.25 = ₹8,400
Step 3: Final price at 12.5% gain
— 8,400 × 1.125 = ₹9,450
Step 4: Rate of the further reduction
— Reduction = 10,500 − 9,450 = ₹1,050
— Rate = 1,050 ÷ 10,500 × 100 = 10%
Step 5: Check a slip
— Subtracting the gains (25 − 12.5 = 12.5%) is wrong, because the second reduction is taken on ₹10,500, not on the cost
∴ Correct answer: (C) 10%
trick: Fix the cost from the first stage; the second rate is always on the reduced price.

explanation:
Step 1: Split the total by month
— January 20% = ₹96,000, February 25% = ₹1,20,000, March 30% = ₹1,44,000, April 25% = ₹1,20,000
Step 2: Find the paint spending
— January 40% of 96,000 = ₹38,400; February ₹48,000; March 25% of 1,44,000 = ₹36,000; April ₹48,000
Step 3: Test each statement
— Paint is lowest in March (₹36,000): true
— April equals February (₹1,20,000 each): not more
— January steel = ₹57,600, not more than ₹60,000
Step 4: Test the last statement
— Total paint = 38,400 + 48,000 + 36,000 + 48,000 = ₹1,70,400 = 35.5% of 4,80,000, not more than 40%
Step 5: Conclusion
— Only the March paint statement follows
∴ Correct answer: (A) The spending on paint was the lowest in March
trick: Turn every percentage into rupees first; then statements are quick to test.

explanation:
Step 1: Spending in March and February
— March = 30% of 4,80,000 = ₹1,44,000; February = 25% = ₹1,20,000
Step 2: Steel in March
— 75% of 1,44,000 = ₹1,08,000
Step 3: Paint in February
— 40% of 1,20,000 = ₹48,000
Step 4: Form the ratio
— 1,08,000 : 48,000 = 108 : 48 = 9 : 4
Step 5: Check a slip
— Using 60% steel in March gives 86,400 : 48,000 = 9 : 5, a wrong option
∴ Correct answer: (B) 9:4
trick: Remember the March exception: steel is 75% only in March.

explanation:
Step 1: Relative speed in opposite directions
— 54 + 36 = 90 km/h
Step 2: Convert to m/s
— 90 × 5 ÷ 18 = 25 m/s
Step 3: Distance to be covered
— Sum of lengths = 280 + 220 = 500 m
Step 4: Time
— 500 ÷ 25 = 20 seconds
Step 5: Check a slip
— Subtracting the speeds (18 km/h = 5 m/s) gives 100 seconds, which is for the same direction
∴ Correct answer: (A) 20 seconds
trick: Opposite directions: add the speeds; distance is the sum of the two lengths.

explanation:
Step 1: Read the values
— Production: B 25%, D 30% of 60,000; unsold: B 20%, D 25%
Step 2: Production of B and D
— B = 25% of 60,000 = 15,000; D = 30% of 60,000 = 18,000
Step 3: Coolers sold
— B sold 80% of 15,000 = 12,000; D sold 75% of 18,000 = 13,500
Step 4: Add
— 12,000 + 13,500 = 25,500
Step 5: Check a slip
— The unsold coolers are 3,000 + 4,500 = 7,500, a trap option
∴ Correct answer: (A) 25,500
trick: Sold = production × (100 − unsold%) ÷ 100 for each plant.

explanation:
Step 1: Production of C
— 15% of 60,000 = 9,000 coolers
Step 2: Split into sold and unsold
— Unsold 15% = 1,350; sold = 9,000 − 1,350 = 7,650
Step 3: Amount from each part
— Sold: 7,650 × 2,400 = ₹1,83,60,000
— Cleared: 1,350 × 1,500 = ₹20,25,000
Step 4: Add and convert
— Total = ₹2,03,85,000 = ₹203.85 lakh
Step 5: Check a slip
— Counting all 9,000 at ₹2,400 gives ₹216 lakh, which ignores the unsold coolers
∴ Correct answer: (C) ₹203.85 lakh
trick: 1 lakh = 1,00,000; split the units first, then price each part.

explanation:
Step 1: Production of A and E
— A = 20% of 60,000 = 12,000; E = 10% of 60,000 = 6,000
Step 2: Unsold of A
— 10% of 12,000 = 1,200
Step 3: Unsold of E
— 5% of 6,000 = 300
Step 4: Form the ratio
— 1,200 : 300 = 4 : 1
Step 5: Check a slip
— Comparing only the unsold percentages (10 : 5) gives 2 : 1, which ignores production
∴ Correct answer: (D) 4:1
trick: Ratio of unsold = (share × unsold%) of one ÷ (share × unsold%) of the other: 20 × 10 : 10 × 5.

explanation:
Step 1: Use the rule for the nth term
— \( a_n = S_n - S_{n-1} \)
Step 2: Find the sum of 20 terms
— S20 = 3 × 400 + 5 × 20 = 1,200 + 100 = 1,300
Step 3: Find the sum of 19 terms
— S19 = 3 × 361 + 5 × 19 = 1,083 + 95 = 1,178
Step 4: Subtract
— 20th term = 1,300 − 1,178 = 122
Step 5: Check with the general term
— \( a_n = 6n + 2 \); 6 × 20 + 2 = 122; also the first term 3 + 5 = 8 = 6 + 2
∴ Correct answer: (D) 122
trick: For Sn = an² + bn, the nth term is 2an + (b − a).

explanation:
Step 1: Read the shares
— 2020 14%, 2021 18%, 2022 20%, 2023 22%, 2024 26% of 25,000
Step 2: Test the rise
— 14, 18, 20, 22, 26 rise every year, so the number qualified rose every year: true
Step 3: Test the half statement
— 2023 + 2024 = 22 + 26 = 48%, which is not more than half
Step 4: Test the other two
— 2021 (18%) is less than 2022 (20%)
— 2020 = 14% of 25,000 = 3,500, which is not fewer than 3,000
Step 5: Conclusion
— Only the statement about a rise every year is correct
∴ Correct answer: (C) The number of candidates who qualified rose every year from 2020 to 2024
trick: With one fixed total, comparing the percentages is the same as comparing the numbers.

explanation:
Step 1: Median AD halves the triangle
— Area of ABD = 84 ÷ 2 = 42 cm²
Step 2: Position of the centroid
— G divides AD in the ratio 2 : 1, so GD is one-third of AD
Step 3: Triangles with the same base BD
— Triangles GBD and ABD share base BD; height of G is one-third of the height of A
Step 4: Area of GBD
— Area GBD = 42 ÷ 3 = 14 cm²
Step 5: Check with the rule
— The three medians cut a triangle into 6 equal parts: 84 ÷ 6 = 14 cm²
∴ Correct answer: (B) 14 cm²
trick: Medians divide a triangle into six triangles of equal area.

explanation:
Step 1: Read the Tuesday values
— Bus 300 at ₹180; Truck 360 at ₹240
Step 2: Toll from buses
— 300 × 180 = ₹54,000
Step 3: Toll from trucks
— 360 × 240 = ₹86,400
Step 4: Add
— 54,000 + 86,400 = ₹1,40,400
Step 5: Check
— Rough: 300 × 200 + 360 × 250 = 60,000 + 90,000, close to ₹1.5 lakh, so ₹1,40,400 is reasonable
∴ Correct answer: (D) ₹1,40,400
trick: Toll = number of vehicles × toll per crossing, row by row.

explanation:
Step 1: Read the Wednesday values
— Cars 1,100 at ₹60; trucks 450 at ₹240
Step 2: New number of cars and trucks
— Cars 1,100 × 1.2 = 1,320; trucks 450 × 0.9 = 405
Step 3: New toll
— Cars 1,320 × 60 = ₹79,200; trucks 405 × 240 = ₹97,200
Step 4: Add
— 79,200 + 97,200 = ₹1,76,400
Step 5: Compare with the actual
— Actual = 1,100 × 60 + 450 × 240 = 66,000 + 1,08,000 = ₹1,74,000; the new total is ₹2,400 more
∴ Correct answer: (D) ₹1,76,400
trick: Change the counts first, then multiply by the toll; never change the toll rate.

explanation:
Step 1: Write the formula
— Mean = A + Σfd ÷ Σf
Step 2: Substitute the values
— A = 45, Σfd = −60, Σf = 40
Step 3: Find the correction
— −60 ÷ 40 = −1.5
Step 4: Mean
— 45 − 1.5 = 43.5
Step 5: Check a slip
— Adding 1.5 instead of subtracting gives 46.5; the negative Σfd pulls the mean below 45
∴ Correct answer: (C) 43.5
trick: A negative Σfd means the true mean is below the assumed mean.

explanation:
Step 1: Identify the two prices
— Tag (marked) price ₹1,800; price charged ₹1,530
Step 2: Find the reduction
— 1,800 − 1,530 = ₹270
Step 3: Rate on the tag price
— 270 ÷ 1,800 × 100 = 15%
Step 4: Result
— The reduction allowed is 15%
Step 5: Check a slip
— Dividing by 1,530 gives 17.6%, but a discount is always taken on the marked price
∴ Correct answer: (B) 15%
trick: Discount % = discount ÷ marked price × 100.

explanation:
Step 1: Read the rows
— Kanpur 420/460/440/500, Lucknow 380/410/450/480, Varanasi 300/280/320/350, Patna 350/390/420/410, Ranchi 260/290/310/340
Step 2: Find the stations that rose every year
— Lucknow and Ranchi rise every year; Kanpur falls in 2023, Varanasi in 2022, Patna in 2024
Step 3: Test the 2024 and 2022 statements
— Varanasi 350 is less than Patna 410 in 2024
— Kanpur rose from 420 to 460 in 2022
Step 4: Test the 2023 statement
— In 2023 Lucknow (450) is highest, not Patna (420)
Step 5: Conclusion
— Only the statement about Lucknow and Ranchi is correct
∴ Correct answer: (C) Lucknow and Ranchi are the only stations whose passengers rose every year
trick: Scan each row left to right once and mark every fall.

explanation:
Step 1: Condition for 2023
— At least 420 in 2023: Kanpur (440), Lucknow (450), Patna (420)
Step 2: Condition for 2024
— At least 450 in 2024: Kanpur (500), Lucknow (480); Patna (410) drops out
Step 3: Read 2021 for these stations
— Kanpur 420, Lucknow 380
Step 4: Average
— (420 + 380) ÷ 2 = 400 thousand
Step 5: Check a slip
— Keeping Patna gives (420 + 380 + 350) ÷ 3 = 383.3 thousand, a wrong option
∴ Correct answer: (C) 400 thousand
trick: “At least 420” includes 420 itself; check both years before averaging.

explanation:
Step 1: The reduced sample space
— Red cards 26 + black face cards 6 = 32 cards (red face cards are already among the 26)
Step 2: Kings in this space
— 2 red kings + 2 black kings = 4
Step 3: Conditional probability
— P = 4 ÷ 32
Step 4: Simplify
— \( \frac{4}{32} = \frac{1}{8} \)
Step 5: Check a slip
— Using all 52 cards gives \( \frac{4}{52} = \frac{1}{13} \), which ignores the given information
∴ Correct answer: (A) \( \frac{1}{8} \)
trick: Given information shrinks the deck: count favourable cards only inside the shrunken deck.

explanation:
Step 1: Read the points
— Monday (4, 5), Tuesday (6, 7), Wednesday (5, 6), Thursday (8, 9), Friday (7, 8), Saturday (10, 12), Sunday (3, 11)
Step 2: Find the common pattern
— On six days the afternoon count is 1 to 2 hundred more than the morning count
Step 3: Test Sunday
— Sunday: afternoon 11 against morning 3, a gap of 8 hundred
Step 4: Identify the outlier
— Sunday lies far above the band of the other points
Step 5: Check Saturday
— Saturday (10, 12) is high but still follows the pattern, with a gap of 2
∴ Correct answer: (B) Sunday
trick: An outlier breaks the trend of the other points; a large value alone is not an outlier.

explanation:
Step 1: Area of the courtyard
— 42 × 42 = 1,764 m²
Step 2: Four quarter circles
— Four quarters of radius 7 m make one circle: \( \frac{22}{7} \) × 7 × 7 = 154 m²
Step 3: The fountain
— \( \frac{22}{7} \) × 14 × 14 = 616 m²
Step 4: Area left
— 1,764 − 154 − 616 = 994 m²
Step 5: Check a slip
— Taking away only the fountain leaves 1,148 m², which forgets the corner beds
∴ Correct answer: (B) 994 m²
trick: Four equal quarter circles at the corners always add up to one full circle.

explanation:
Step 1: Write the identity
— \( x^3 + \frac{1}{x^3} = \left(x + \frac{1}{x}\right)^3 - 3\left(x + \frac{1}{x}\right) \)
Step 2: Cube the given value
— 5 × 5 × 5 = 125
Step 3: Three times the value
— 3 × 5 = 15
Step 4: Subtract
— 125 − 15 = 110
Step 5: Check a slip
— Stopping at the cube gives 125, which leaves out the middle terms
∴ Correct answer: (C) 110
trick: If x + 1/x = k, then x³ + 1/x³ = k³ − 3k.

explanation:
Step 1: Work of the two taps in 1 hour
— \( \frac{1}{10} + \frac{1}{15} = \frac{1}{6} \), so together they fill it in 6 h
Step 2: Time with the hole
— 6 + 2 = 8 h, so the net filling is \( \frac{1}{8} \) per hour
Step 3: Work of the hole in 1 hour
— \( \frac{1}{6} - \frac{1}{8} = \frac{1}{24} \)
Step 4: Time for the hole alone
— The hole drains the full cistern in 24 h
Step 5: Check
— In 8 h the taps fill \( \frac{8}{6} \) and the hole drains \( \frac{8}{24} \); the difference is exactly 1 cistern
∴ Correct answer: (C) 24 h
trick: Leak rate = (filling rate without leak) − (filling rate with leak).

explanation:
Step 1: Read the bars
— Q1-2023 360, Q2-2023 420, Q3-2023 480, Q4-2023 390, Q1-2024 450, Q2-2024 510
Step 2: Apply the condition
— More than 400 and less than 500: 420, 480 and 450
Step 3: Leave out the rest
— 360 and 390 are not more than 400; 510 is not less than 500
Step 4: Average
— (420 + 480 + 450) ÷ 3 = 1,350 ÷ 3 = 450 tonnes
Step 5: Check a slip
— Keeping 510 gives (1,350 + 510) ÷ 4 = 465 tonnes, a wrong option
∴ Correct answer: (D) 450 tonnes
trick: Filter with both ends of the range, then average only what is left.

explanation:
Step 1: Formula for the sum of squares
— Sum = n(n + 1)(2n + 1) ÷ 6
Step 2: Substitute n = 8
— 8 × 9 × 17 ÷ 6 = 1,224 ÷ 6 = 204
Step 3: Average
— 204 ÷ 8 = 25.5
Step 4: Result
— The average of the squares is 25.5
Step 5: Check
— 1 + 4 + 9 + 16 + 25 + 36 + 49 + 64 = 204; 204 is the sum, not the average
∴ Correct answer: (D) 25.5
trick: Average of the first n squares = (n + 1)(2n + 1) ÷ 6 = 9 × 17 ÷ 6.

explanation:
Step 1: Write the variation
— Days ∝ work ÷ (workers × machines²)
Step 2: Factor for each change
— Work × 2; workers × 1.5; machines × 2, so machines² × 4
Step 3: Combine the factors
— New days = 48 × 2 ÷ (1.5 × 4) = 96 ÷ 6
Step 4: Result
— 16 days
Step 5: Check a slip
— Forgetting to square the machines gives 96 ÷ 3 = 32 days, a wrong option
∴ Correct answer: (B) 16 days
trick: Multiply by the factor for direct variation and divide by it for inverse variation.

explanation:
Step 1: Convert degrees to books
— 1° = 7,200 ÷ 360 = 20 books
Step 2: August and September
— August 54° = 1,080 books; September 81° = 1,620 books
Step 3: Rise
— 1,620 − 1,080 = 540 books
Step 4: Percentage rise
— 540 ÷ 1,080 × 100 = 50%
Step 5: Shortcut check
— Degrees alone: (81 − 54) ÷ 54 × 100 = 27 ÷ 54 × 100 = 50%
∴ Correct answer: (D) 50%
trick: A percentage change can be found from the degrees directly; the total cancels.

explanation:
Step 1: What must be decided
— Whether x is a multiple of 6, a yes or no question
Step 2: Statement I alone
— 12 = 6 × 2, so every multiple of 12 is a multiple of 6: the answer is a definite yes
Step 3: Statement II alone
— x even: 12 is divisible by 6 but 8 is not, so no definite answer
Step 4: Decide
— Statement I alone is sufficient
Step 5: Check a slip
— Thinking both are needed is wrong, because I already settles the question
∴ Correct answer: (A) Statement I alone is sufficient
trick: In a yes or no question, a statement is sufficient if it gives the same answer in every case.

explanation:
Step 1: Take a cost price
— Let CP = ₹100
Step 2: Marked price
— 40% above cost: MP = ₹140
Step 3: Selling price
— 15% discount: SP = 140 × 0.85 = ₹119
Step 4: Profit percentage
— Profit = 119 − 100 = ₹19, that is 19%
Step 5: Check a slip
— Subtracting the rates (40 − 15 = 25%) is wrong; the discount is on 140, not on 100
∴ Correct answer: (A) 19%

Step 1: Monthly expenses
— 7,500 + 3,500 = ₹11,000
Step 2: Monthly saving
— 28,000 − 11,000 = ₹17,000
Step 3: Months in which she saves
— One month is spent on gifts, so she saves in 12 − 1 = 11 months
Step 4: Yearly savings
— 17,000 × 11 = ₹1,87,000
Step 5: Check a slip
— Counting all 12 months gives ₹2,04,000, which ignores the wedding month
∴ Correct answer: (B) ₹1,87,000
trick: Saving per month × number of months actually saved.

explanation:
Step 1: Take the investments as units
— A 3, B 4, C 5 units
Step 2: Effective capital of A
— 3 × 4 + 6 × 8 = 12 + 48 = 60
Step 3: Effective capital of B and C
— B: 4 × 12 = 48
— C: 5 × 4 + 3 × 8 = 20 + 24 = 44 (40% of 5 withdrawn leaves 3)
Step 4: Ratio
— 60 : 48 : 44 = 15 : 12 : 11
Step 5: Check
— 15 + 12 + 11 = 38 parts; 60 + 48 + 44 = 152 = 38 × 4, so the ratio is consistent
∴ Correct answer: (D) 15:12:11
trick: Effective capital = amount × months, added over each period.

explanation:
Step 1: Read the shares
— Operations 28, Engineering 22, Mechanical 18, Electrical 15, Commercial 10, Medical 7 (%)
Step 2: Apply the condition
— At least 15% and less than 25%: Engineering 22, Mechanical 18, Electrical 15
Step 3: Add the shares
— 22 + 18 + 15 = 55%
Step 4: Convert to employees
— 55% of 4,800 = 2,640
Step 5: Check a slip
— Leaving out Electrical (exactly 15%) gives 40% = 1,920; at least 15% includes 15
∴ Correct answer: (B) 2,640
trick: Add the percentages that pass the filter, then convert once.

explanation:
Step 1: Formula
— Curved surface area of a cylinder = 2πrh
Step 2: Substitute
— 2 × \( \frac{22}{7} \) × 1.4 × 2 = 17.6 m²
Step 3: Cost
— 17.6 × 50 = ₹880
Step 4: Result
— The painting costs ₹880
Step 5: Check a slip
— Adding the two ends (2πr² = 12.32 m²) gives 29.92 m² and ₹1,496, but only the curved surface is painted
∴ Correct answer: (C) ₹880
trick: Curved surface only: 2πrh; total surface adds 2πr².

explanation:
Step 1: Read the marks
— Test 1 48, Test 2 60, Test 3 66, Test 4 55, Test 5 77
Step 2: Percentage change for each step
— 1 to 2: 12 ÷ 48 = 25%
— 2 to 3: 6 ÷ 60 = 10%
— 3 to 4: a fall of 11 marks
Step 3: Last step
— 4 to 5: 22 ÷ 55 = 40%
Step 4: Compare
— 40% is the highest increase: Test 4 to Test 5
Step 5: Note
— The rise from 55 is large because the base is small after the fall
∴ Correct answer: (C) Test 4 to Test 5
trick: Percentage increase = rise ÷ earlier value × 100; a fall can never be the answer.

explanation:
Step 1: Difference in time
— 6 minutes late and 4 minutes early: difference = 10 minutes = \( \frac{1}{6} \) hour
Step 2: Form the equation
— \( \frac{d}{5} - \frac{d}{6} = \frac{1}{6} \)
Step 3: Solve
— \( \frac{d}{30} = \frac{1}{6} \), so d = 30 ÷ 6 = 5 km
Step 4: Result
— The distance is 5 km
Step 5: Check
— At 5 km/h: 60 minutes; at 6 km/h: 50 minutes; the difference is 10 minutes
∴ Correct answer: (B) 5 km
trick: Late plus early gives the total time difference; distance = product of speeds × time gap ÷ difference of speeds.

explanation:
Step 1: Static friction
— Before a body moves, static friction rises up to its limiting value, the largest of the three
Step 2: Sliding friction
— Once the body slides, the friction is a little less than the limiting static friction
Step 3: Rolling friction
— A rolling wheel touches the surface over a very small area, so rolling friction is the smallest
Step 4: Order
— Static, then sliding, then rolling, from largest to smallest
Step 5: Link to the railways
— This is why wheels and ball bearings are used to move heavy loads
∴ Correct answer: (A) Static friction, then sliding friction, then rolling friction, from largest to smallest
trick: Starting is hardest, sliding is easier, rolling is easiest.

explanation:
Step 1: Condition for no solution
— a1 ÷ a2 = b1 ÷ b2, but not equal to c1 ÷ c2
Step 2: Ratio of the y-coefficients
— (−2) ÷ (−6) = \( \frac{1}{3} \)
Step 3: Ratio of the x-coefficients
— \( \frac{5}{k} = \frac{1}{3} \), so k = 15
Step 4: Check the constants
— 9 ÷ 20 is not equal to \( \frac{1}{3} \), so the lines are parallel and distinct
Step 5: Result
— k = 15
∴ Correct answer: (C) 15
trick: Parallel lines: x and y coefficients in the same ratio, constants in a different ratio.

explanation:
Step 1: What is needed
— Class average = (boys × boys average + girls × girls average) ÷ total students
Step 2: Statement I
— 40 students, 25 boys, so 15 girls: gives the weights only
Step 3: Statements II and III
— Boys average 62 and girls average 70: give the two averages

explanation:
Explanation:
— The passage gives the traditional reading (‘a lesson in devotion’) and then a modern one (‘the gatekeeping of skill’).
— It says ‘Neither reading is entirely wrong’, so the theme must hold both readings together.
— ‘Eklavya was the greatest archer’ is too narrow and goes beyond the text, which says only that his skill rivalled the finest prince.
— ‘Modern readers have completely rejected the traditional reading’ contradicts the line that neither reading is wrong.
— So the theme is that the story can be read both as praise of devotion and as a record of talent denied a fair chance.
∴ Correct answer: (C) The Eklavya story can be read both as praise of devotion and as a record of talent being denied a fair chance
trick: A central theme must cover the whole passage, including its turn and its close.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The line is: ‘makes a clay image of the master and practises before it’.
— A detail question asks only what the passage states.
— ‘Receiving lessons from Drona in the forest’ fails because Eklavya was ‘refused instruction’.
— ‘Training secretly with the royal princes’ and ‘copying a favoured pupil’ are never mentioned.
— So he learnt by practising before a clay image of his teacher.
∴ Correct answer: (B) practising before a clay image of his teacher
trick: Find the exact sentence; reject options that add facts.

explanation:
Explanation:
— Gatekeeping is defined as institutions protecting rank ‘by denying opportunity’ to talent that grew ‘without privilege’.
— An application question asks for a new situation with the same structure.
— The club that keeps a gifted outsider off the team so members’ children keep their places has exactly that structure.
— The scholarship won on merit shows talent rewarded, the opposite of the author’s point.
— Free lessons to a poor pupil open opportunity, and an injury has nothing to do with rank; so the club case is the answer.
∴ Correct answer: (C) A sports club keeps a gifted outsider off its team so that its members’ children keep their places
trick: Match the structure (who is kept out, and why), not the setting.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The passage opens with the usual telling: ‘usually told as a lesson in devotion’.
— It turns with ‘Yet many modern readers find the same episode troubling’, a contrasting reading.
— It closes by saying the unease is ‘its lasting value’ and the story ‘keeps returning’.
— ‘Argues that the traditional reading is false’ fails, because the author says ‘Neither reading is entirely wrong’.
— It does not list events in order or compare regional versions; so it recounts, contrasts and explains why the tension lasts.
∴ Correct answer: (D) It recounts a traditional story with its usual lesson, offers a contrasting modern reading and closes by explaining why the tension keeps the story alive
trick: Trace the signal words (usually, Yet, Perhaps) to see the shape of the passage.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The phrase is talent ‘deliberately cut short so that a favoured pupil might remain unrivalled’.
— ‘So that’ shows a purpose, so the act was done on purpose.
— ‘Intentionally’ means on purpose, which fits exactly.
— ‘Secretly’ fails, because the fee was asked for openly; ‘carelessly’ is the opposite of on purpose.
— ‘Slowly’ has nothing to do with purpose; so the closest synonym is ‘intentionally’.
∴ Correct answer: (A) Intentionally
trick: Read the whole sentence; the purpose clause gives away the meaning.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The line is: ‘Because its reasoning is often hidden inside layers of calculation, an unfair outcome may go unnoticed for months’.
— A detail question takes the reason exactly as given.
— ‘It applies different rules to different cases’ contradicts the passage, which says it applies ‘the same rule to every case’.
— ‘Works more slowly than a clerk’ contradicts ‘they work quickly’.
— Nothing says reviewers cannot see the decisions; so the hidden reasoning is the answer.
∴ Correct answer: (A) its reasoning is often hidden inside layers of calculation
trick: Look for the word “because” in the passage; it usually carries the reason asked.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The passage moves from the appeal of automated systems to their weakness, then to the need for a person ‘in the loop’.
— It ends on what makes oversight real: ‘time, training and genuine authority’.
— A good title must cover both the need for oversight and the condition that it be real.
— ‘How Banks Approve Loans’ covers one example only, and ‘Pilots and Co-pilots’ is just an analogy.
— ‘The End of Human Judgement’ contradicts the passage; so the title about keeping a human in the loop fits best.
∴ Correct answer: (B) Keeping a Human in the Loop: Why Automated Decisions Need Real Oversight
trick: A title is the theme in a few words; reject examples and analogies.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The passage grants the strengths of automated systems (‘their appeal is easy to understand’).
— It names the weakness of hidden bias and argues for human oversight.
— It closes: ‘Effective oversight therefore depends on giving reviewers time, training and genuine authority’.
— ‘Automated systems are always biased and should be banned’ goes too far; the passage never calls for a ban.
— ‘Machines should replace clerks’ and ‘training is the costliest part’ are not argued; so the balanced theme is correct.
∴ Correct answer: (D) Automated decision systems are useful but need meaningful human oversight, which must itself be properly supported
trick: Prefer the option that keeps both sides the author weighs.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The author weighs strengths against costs: ‘It does, however, carry costs’.
— The language is measured, with reasons for each claim and no exclamations.
— ‘Enthusiastic and celebratory’ fails, because the weaknesses are stressed as much as the strengths.
— ‘Sceptical and dismissive’ fails, because oversight is ‘not a sign of distrust in technology’.
— There is no emotional or gloomy language; so the tone is objective and analytical.
∴ Correct answer: (C) Objective and analytical
trick: Balanced reasons with no strong feeling point to an objective, analytical tone.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The passage says a reviewer who ‘checks thousands of cases may begin to approve whatever the system suggests’.
— It adds that oversight needs ‘genuine authority’ to remain ‘a real judgement rather than a signature’.
— So an overloaded reviewer without power may add little protection: this follows from the text.
— ‘Automated systems never make mistakes once well trained’ contradicts the point about absorbed biases.
— Nothing ranks co-pilots above pilots or calls for removing reviewers; so the first inference is correct.
∴ Correct answer: (A) A reviewer with too many cases and no real authority may add little protection against the system’s errors
trick: An inference must follow from stated lines without adding new claims.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The phrase is: ‘More durable answers seem to combine respect for tradition with practical support’.
— It follows the line about efforts that ‘backfired’, so durable answers are those that hold up over time.
— ‘Lasting’ means holding up over time, which fits.
— ‘Temporary’ is the opposite meaning, and ‘costly’ or ‘attractive’ do not fit the contrast with efforts that failed.
— So the closest synonym is ‘lasting’.
∴ Correct answer: (D) Lasting
trick: Use the contrast with the sentence before to fix the meaning.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The author values the craft as ‘a living record of local identity’.
— He also faces the problem plainly: ‘identity alone does not pay the weaver’.
— He weighs remedies calmly and ends with a general reflection, without anger or praise.
— ‘Urgent and confrontational’ fails, because no one is attacked; ‘humorous and ironic’ has no support.
— ‘Enthusiastic and celebratory’ ignores the difficulties; so the tone is reflective and balanced.
∴ Correct answer: (B) Reflective and balanced
trick: Both value and difficulty in calm language: reflective and balanced.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The passage says some efforts made weavers change designs ‘so completely to suit distant buyers that the cloth loses the very distinctiveness that made it valuable’.
— So a design changed beyond recognition may end up lowering the cloth’s value: this follows directly.
— ‘Machine-made copies are better in quality’ is never said; they are only cheaper.
— ‘Young people dislike their traditions’ goes beyond the text, which says only that they prefer steadier work.
— ‘Protected names alone will solve all problems’ is too strong, since the author lists several measures together.
∴ Correct answer: (C) A design changed beyond recognition to please distant buyers may end up lowering the value of the cloth
trick: Watch for options with “all”, “alone” or “better”; they usually overstate.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The passage links handwoven cloth to regional identity and asks how weaving can survive.
— Its answer is support that adapts ‘without erasing the core motifs’, keeping the character of the cloth.
— ‘Woven Identity: Keeping Handloom Alive Without Losing Its Character’ covers both ideas.
— ‘Young People Move to Towns’ is one detail, and ‘The History of the Indian Sari’ is not discussed.
— ‘Why Machines Make Better Cloth’ contradicts the passage; so the first title fits best.
∴ Correct answer: (D) Woven Identity: Keeping Handloom Alive Without Losing Its Character
trick: The best title names the problem and the balance the author wants.

explanation:
Explanation:
— The close is: ‘A tradition, after all, survives only if those who carry it can also make a living from it’.
— For this to hold, the author must assume that people will not keep up a craft that cannot support them.
— So the assumption is that a tradition is unlikely to continue if practising it cannot give an adequate income.
— ‘Every weaver wants to move to a town’ goes too far; the passage says only ‘many young people’.
— ‘Traditions never change’ contradicts the support for adapting colours or uses; ‘buyers do not care about price’ contradicts the cheap copies.
∴ Correct answer: (D) A craft tradition is unlikely to continue if practising it cannot give an adequate income
trick: An assumption is the unstated link the conclusion needs; test by negating it.
